title: Interpreting the $γ$-ray emission from Westerlund 1: hadronic or leptonic?
summary: High-energy $γ$-ray emission has been detected from several star clusters, indicating that these sources are sites of cosmic-ray acceleration. However, it is still unclear whether the $γ$-ray emission is of hadronic or leptonic origin. We present a comprehensive study of the $γ$-ray emission from Westerlund 1, under the assumption that high-energy particles are accelerated at the cluster WTS. We investigate both the hadronic and leptonic scenarios by fitting simultaneously the spectrum and morphology of the $γ$-ray emission. We numerically solve the transport equations for non-thermal protons and electrons for a given $K_\mathrm{ep}$ and derive their energy and spatial distributions. $γ$ rays are produced either by hadronic pp interactions of protons with the target gas or by inverse Compton scattering of relativistic electrons (both primary and secondary) with the ambient photon fields. We also calculate the synchrotron emission from these electrons. The predicted SEDs are compared with the $γ$-ray measurements by Fermi-LAT and HESS and with the X-ray upper limit derived by eROSITA. For reasonable model parameters, we find that in the case of Bohm diffusion, both the leptonic and hadronic scenarios can account for the observed multi-wavelength spectrum and $γ$-ray morphology. However, in the case of Kraichnan diffusion, better motivated in star clusters, only the hadronic scenario can explain the observations, while the leptonic scenario fails to reproduce the highest-energy $γ$-ray data points. For the leptonic scenario, the magnetic field immediately downstream of the shock can be constrained to be $\lesssim$ a few $μ$G thanks to the eROSITA upper limit. On the other hand, in order to explain the $γ$-ray observations with hadronic emission alone, the gas density inside the bubble should be $\gtrsim 1.2 \, \rm{cm}^{-3}$.

title: Ammonia Fitting of Multiple Velocity Components in High-Mass Star-Forming Regions
summary: We perform a multiple velocity component analysis of ammonia (NH$_3$) gas from KEYSTONE, a Green Bank Telescope survey covering 11 giant molecular clouds (GMCs) at distances from 0.7 to 2.7 kpc. We extend existing codes to enable simultaneous fitting of up to three velocity components in NH$_3$ (1,1) with radiative transfer. Using our multiple component fitting technique, we produce the best maps of the centroid velocity and velocity dispersion in these clouds to date. Over the entire survey, multiple velocity components were seen in 13% of pixels where we detect and fit NH$_3$ emission, primarily in clusters at the heart of the GMCs. In these multiple component pixels, the median measured NH$_3$ linewidth decreased by a factor of 1.4 compared to equivalent single-component measurements, but there are also significant cloud-to-cloud variations. Regions with multiple velocity components tend to be found in the densest zones of the GMCs and at the sites of high-mass star formation, indicative of multiple filaments, cores, or complex velocities associated with the formation of massive stars. Disentangling these velocity features will allow future quantitative analysis of coherent motions, such as infall and outflow, in these complex environments. The multi-component data products are available on the CADC.

title: The Milky Way's Early Disk Was Built in Bursts. II. The Multi-component Age-Metallicity Structure of the High-$α$ Disk
summary: Whether the high-$α$ disk experienced a continuous or episodic star-formation history remains an open question. Here we investigate the age--metallicity distribution of the high-$α$ disk using approximately 145,000 Gaia DR3 subgiants with $[\mathrm{Fe/H}]>-1$, 6.5~kpc $\lesssim R\lesssim9.5$~kpc, and $|Z|\lesssim1.5$~kpc. We adopt a forward-modelling framework that accounts for individual age and metallicity uncertainties and corrects for sample selection effects. The reconstructed distribution reveals two components: a broad, dominant population peaking at $\sim10.6$ Gyr and $[\mathrm{Fe/H}]\simeq-0.38$, and an older, more metal-poor population peaking at $\sim12.4$ Gyr and $[\mathrm{Fe/H}]\simeq-0.79$. These features suggest an episodic history of star formation and chemical enrichment in the high-$α$ disk, qualitatively consistent with cosmological simulations in which recurrent gas accretion drives variations in the star formation rate. The age of the older component is close to the $\sim12.3$~Gyr epoch inferred for the proposed Low-energy--Kraken--Heracles accretion event, suggesting a possible connection between this early interaction and enhanced disk star formation. There is tentative evidence that the dominant population is possibly composed of two sub-components with age distributions peaking at $\sim11.1$ Gyr and $\sim10.0$ Gyr, respectively. Together, these results favour a picture in which the high-$α$ disk was built through recurrent episodes of enhanced star formation rather than a single temporally smooth phase, even for the regime of ${\rm [Fe/H]}>-1$.

title: Radio and high-energy variable emission from a multi-wavelength follow-up of the infant planet-hosting star V1298 Tau
summary: V1298 Tau is a very young and magnetically active K1V star which hosts a benchmark multi-planetary system to study planet formation and evolutionary history at the earliest stages. Between 2025 and 2026, we conducted a campaign to monitor the variability of V1298 Tau in radio (band C), X-ray, and NUV bands, with the support of publicly available contemporary optical light curve, and to investigate multi-band correlations to link the emission with stellar activity. Radio observations were carried out with the Karl G. Jansky Very Large Array (JVLA) in band C (4.5--6.5 GHz). X-ray and NUV observations were carried out with the Swift satellite over 20 days, ending one month before the begin of the radio campaign. We analysed the temporal variability of peak (integrated) fluxes in the C-band and of X-ray (NUV) luminosities on various timescales, comparing it with the variability observed in the high-cadence optical light curve collected by the ASAS-SN survey. We observed both radio and high-energy time variable emission. JVLA detected emission in 90\% of the visits, switching between high ($\geq$0.1 mJy/beam) and low flux states in matter of days or hours. The fluxes show moderate correlation with the optical light curve, suggesting modulation with the stellar rotation period. Except for one visit, dynamic spectral analysis does not reveal short-term (minutes) variability, nor is there any evidence of circularly polarised emissions. Overall, the radio observations can be explained as gyrosynchrotron and/or cyclotron emission from the corona, and linked to stellar magnetic activity. At high-energy, we detected significant variability in X-ray luminosity (within the range ~1.2--2.5x10$^{+30}$ erg/s), the decay phase of a stellar flare, and evidence of correlation with the optical flux. Our data confirm that V1298\,Tau follows the near-linear Güdel-Benz relation.

title: On the Evolution of Circumstellar Disks Modified by the Presence of a Binary
summary: Stars form within circumstellar disks, and some binary stars develop circumbinary disks surrounding the pair. Observations suggest that disks that form around binary star systems are less common than those around single stars. One possible explanation is that binary stars may disrupt or shorten the lifespan of their surrounding disks relative to those around single stars. To investigate this, we used the DISCO hydrodynamics code to compute the lifetimes of circumstellar disks with and without a binary. Our results indicate that binary systems can reduce the lifetime of a circumbinary disk by a modest factor of two to three compared to disks around single stars. This effect is present when the binary separation is at least one-tenth of the disk radius. While our findings show that binaries can shorten circumbinary disk lifetimes, this alone might not be enough to fully account for the scarcity of these disks.

title: An HST survey of photometry and multiplicity of brown dwarfs and planetary-mass objects in the field of Taurus
summary: We present a photometric and multiplicity survey of 26 young objects with masses between 6 Mj and 37 Mj and spectral type later than M8 in the Taurus star-forming region with the Hubble Space Telescope. We search for companion candidates using two methods: a dedicated photometric technique based on the combination of colours from multi-band photometry and point spread function fitting. No companion candidates are detected beyond 30 au. With an updated membership and age identification, we determine luminosity, temperature, and mass for the 26 young objects using evolutionary models. We demonstrate that our HST observations are sensitive to companions down to masses of 1 Mj and even lower for some targets by artificial star injection tests. After survey completeness correction, we derive a binary frequency < 6.5% for this sample in the 68% confidence interval for companions with mass ratios between 0.1 and 1 and separations between 30 and 7,000 au. We find no significant difference in binary frequency among planetary-mass objects in Taurus, Upper Scorpius, and the field. These findings support that the binary frequency of planetary-mass objects is settled at young ages, probably younger than 1--10 Myr, suggesting that the formation of wide-orbit planetary-mass binaries is inefficient and the disruption of them likely occurs at a very early stage in a low density environment.

title: Chemical Demographics of Star-forming Regions
summary: Our understanding of complex organic chemistry during the formation of stars and planets is shaped by a handful of cherry-picked sources with bright molecular emission lines. This observational bias impedes our assessment of how universal chemical complexity is during star formation. The lack of systematic wideband spectral surveys for statistically significant samples of protostars and cores is a major roadblock to properly probing how COM inventories and abundances depend on the vast range of physical conditions, local cloud and global galactic environments, and evolutionary timescales of low- and high-mass star formation. In turn, this limits our ability to constrain and test physicochemical models, which depend critically on these parameters. The next-generation ALMA2040, with a 10x improvement in line sensitivity, is required to observe COMs, that we perceive as common today, in a fraction of the observing time that is needed today with ALMA. Such capabilities will propel us into the era of chemical demographics, whereby wideband (>100 GHz) spectral surveys at high sensitivity (routinely probing COM abundances down to 0.01% relative to CH3OH) will be executed towards >1000-10000 prestellar and protostellar sources. With robust chemical inventories towards large source sample sizes, we will be able to probe for dependencies of chemical complexity on mass regime, feedback processes in a cluster, Galactic position, metallicity, and time-variable accretion. Only with statistically significant samples at high sensitivity will we be able to assess the ubiquity and homogeneity of COM chemistry across the protostellar mass spectrum and natal cores. Constraining the diversity and availability of such species is critical for our understanding of the chemical reservoir available for planet formation, which eventually shapes (exo)planetary atmosphere compositions.

title: Demographics of Close-In TESS Exoplanets Orbiting FGK Main-sequence Stars II. Spectral-Type Dependence and the Neptunian Landscape
summary: Understanding how planetary demographics depend on host star properties is essential for constraining planet formation and evolution theories. In this paper, we analyse close-in 0.5-16 d planet occurrence rates from the TESS Science Processing Operations Center (SPOC) full-frame image data for individual F-, G-, and K-type main-sequence stellar samples. Integrated over $0.5 < P < 16$ d and $2 < R_\mathrm{p} < 20\,R_\oplus$, the occurrence rates are $12.1^{+3.0}_{-2.3}$, $10.2^{+1.2}_{-1.0}$, and $13.1^{+1.4}_{-1.2}$ planets per 100 stars for F-, G-, and K-type hosts, consistent with each other at $1σ$, so any spectral-type dependence is localized rather than global. For transiting hot Jupiters, we measure $0.30^{+0.04}_{-0.03}$, $0.50\pm0.03$, and $0.67^{+0.08}_{-0.07}$ per cent, with the rate peaking at K type; the latter being the first such measurement for K-type hosts. Modelling the Neptunian desert directly in occurrence-rate space, we find that the desert extends to longer orbital periods around hotter stars. Integrating over the desert interior gives $0.069^{+0.045}_{-0.011}$, $0.093^{+0.046}_{-0.022}$, and $0.150^{+0.033}_{-0.026}$ planets per 100 stars, implying about one close-in planet in a hundred lies inside the desert, and the desert is roughly twice as populated around K- as around F-type hosts. A rigorous Bayesian model comparison for the $6$-$8\,R_\oplus$ strip indicates that a distinct Neptunian ridge is not required to explain the measurements.

title: EK Cha b: multi-tracer detection of a protoplanet candidate in a gas-rich environment
summary: Despite sustained community efforts and advances in instrumentation and high-contrast imaging, the search for protoplanets remains difficult, with only two widely accepted systems to date in Class II systems (PDS 70 and WISPIT 2). Here we present the detection of EK Cha b, a new protoplanet candidate, identified through CO emission, millimeter continuum and 0.82 micron broadband photometry, linked to EK Cha, a young late-type M star. The detection of a new protoplanet candidate offers an additional opportunity to advance our understanding of planet formation. By exploiting the wealth of archival data available for nearby star-forming regions, we aim to place EK Cha b in context, characterize its properties, and motivate future campaigns targeting similar systems. We analyzed high-spatial-resolution archival observations of EK Cha from HST, VLT/NACO, VLT/MUSE, and ALMA. We searched for EK Cha b in broadband continuum and gas tracers, reporting the measured flux with uncertainties, and upper limits for non-detections. EK Cha b shows a spectrally-resolved footprint that matches the CO J=2--1 emission, together with 0.82 micron and millimeter continuum emission. EK Cha b is spectrally resolved in CO J=2--1 emission, kinematically consistent with a circumplanetary disk. Best fits from evolutionary models place EK Cha b as a planetary mass companion, although deeper observations are required to fully confirm its nature. Although giant planets are uncommon around M dwarfs, these stars host the highest planet occurrence rate while remaining severely underrepresented in protoplanet searches. EK Cha b demonstrates that such systems are now within reach, and the advent of extremely large telescopes and improved high-contrast imaging -- where the lower host luminosity relaxes the required contras-- will open this overlooked regime to systematic exploration.

title: Global and Local Infall in the ASHES Sample (GLASHES). III. Physical Parameters of Contracting Motion onto Dense Cores in 70 $μ$m Dark Massive Clumps
summary: Core growth is a key process in high-mass star formation. As part of the GLASHES (Global and Local Infall in the ASHES Sample) survey, we present infall velocities and mass infall rates derived from blue-asymmetric line profiles toward cores embedded in massive 70 \textmu m-dark clumps. Robust Hill5 model fits were obtained for 70 of the 135 cores exhibiting blue-asymmetric profiles, yielding infall velocities of 0.11--1.60 km s$^{-1}$ and mass infall rates ranging from $\sim$10$^{-5}$ to $5\times10^{-3}\,M_\odot\,{\rm yr}^{-1}$. Both quantities increase systematically from prestellar candidates to warm cores and outflow-associated cores. The inferred infall velocities are close to the cores' free-fall velocities (mean $v_{\rm in}/v_{\rm ff}\sim0.75$) and $t_{\rm in}=R/v_{\rm in}$ is comparable to the free-fall time, indicating dynamical fast contraction. Hill5 infall velocity correlates moderately with the non-thermal velocity dispersion and Mach number measured from optically thin tracers, indicating that organized infall contributes to the observed line widths. The mass infall rate follows a power-law relation with core mass, $\dot{M}=1.3\times10^{-4}\,(M/M_\odot)^{0.83\pm 0.06}\,M_\odot\,{\rm yr}^{-1}$, across $0.1\,M_\odot \lesssim M \lesssim 30\,M_\odot$. The power-law index increases from $\sim$0.65 for prestellar cores to $\sim$1.10 for outflow-associated cores, likely tracing an evolution in the dominant physical process. The Hill5 infall velocities and mass infall rates for the GLASHES cores are larger than those of cores in nearby low-mass star forming regions but smaller than those of larger scale high-mass clumps. These results provide the first statistical constraints on core-scale mass accumulation during the earliest stages of high-mass star formation.

title: Cracking open the "dragon egg": ALMA 1.3mm observations of a compact, young high-mass core candidate at 30mas resolution
summary: Massive prestellar cores are a central assumption of core-accretion models of high-mass star formation, yet convincing observational examples remain rare. The "dragon egg" (C2c1a) core in the infrared-dark cloud G028.37+00.07 has been proposed as a promising compact high-mass core candidate. We present new ALMA Band 6 observations at $0.035''$-$0.078''$ ($\sim175$-400 au at 5 kpc), providing one of the most stringent high-resolution tests of such a candidate. The region resolves into multiple fragments, but the brightest component, C2c1a(a), remains a single compact continuum peak down to $\sim175$ au, with a deconvolved radius of $\sim87$ au and a nearest neighbouring fragment at a projected separation of $\sim2400$ au. The continuum peak reaches a brightness temperature of $\sim40$ K, exceeding the $\sim10$ K gas temperatures inferred from lower-resolution NH$_3$ observations and indicating a strong radial temperature gradient. Continuum-based mass estimates range from $\sim2$ to $\sim30$ $M_\odot$ (implying extreme densities of $n_\mathrm{H2} > 10^9$cm$^{-3}$), depending on temperature, while lower-resolution data indicate a much larger mass reservoir of $\sim110$ $M_\odot$ on $\sim10^4$ au scales. The spectrum shows no strong hot-core tracers and only weak, spatially extended H$_2$CO and CO emission; no high-velocity outflow can be unambiguously associated with C2c1a(a). We conclude that C2c1a(a) is an exceptionally compact core embedded within a massive cold reservoir, with no additional compact fragments detected within the present resolution and sensitivity limits, potentially tracing the earliest formation of a central protostellar "seed" within a still-dominant reservoir. [abridged]

title: DEMOS I. A Bayesian inference framework to constrain disc evolution from observed demographics
summary: The mechanism driving the evolution and dispersal of protoplanetary discs has a substantial impact on the theories of planet formation. To date, neither the viscous paradigm nor the MHD wind-driven framework have been ruled out by the observations. The statistical richness of the observed samples provides a unique opportunity to test evolutionary models through population synthesis. However, comparisons between models and observations are normally carried out by eye, and a more statistically rigorous approach has not yet been implemented. We present DEMOS, a Bayesian inference tool that aims to infer the model parameters and initial conditions that best reproduce the full distribution of global properties of disc populations. This framework relies on a comparison between observations and synthetic populations generated with the 1D disc population-synthesis code Diskpop. We tested the tool with both the MHD wind model and the viscous framework with internal photoevaporation. Applying DEMOS to synthetic populations, we find that, for both models, it accurately recovers the model parameters of disc populations and their associated uncertainties, including cases in which initial conditions are correlated with the stellar mass. In the optimal scenario in which disc masses, accretion rates and disc sizes are available, the tool can also constrain the angular-momentum transport parameter. We show that, although parameter estimates are the most precise with samples of about 100 discs, the tool also yields meaningful constraints for smaller populations of 10-30 discs. We further find that the predictions obtained with DEMOS closely align with those found by previous works. We anticipate that DEMOS will be a valuable tool to infer the initial conditions of observed disc populations, to design observational programmes, and to assess which evolutionary model best reproduces the data.

title: HD 152384: A 5 Myr old debris disk system showing a gaseous ring of refractory elements at the dust sublimation radius
summary: Context: Circumstellar gas around young stars provides key insights into planet formation and disk evolution. HD 152384, a young (5 Myr) A0 V star in Sco-Cen, shows hybrid-disk traits: a modest infrared excess from small dust grains and atomic emission lines dominated by refractory elements, but its disk structure and origin remain unclear. Aims: We characterise the kinematics and excitation of the circumstellar gas around HD 152384 and constrain the physical properties of its emitting region. Methods: We use new high-resolution optical and near-infrared VLT/UVES and VLT/CRIRES spectra to re-examine the circumstellar environment of HD 152384, previously suggested to host a broad, gas-rich disk. Results: The observations reveal 74 narrow, double-peaked emission lines of Fe, Mg, Si, and Ca, with similar profiles and a 103 km/s peak separation. Keplerian modelling places the gas in a geometrically thin ring at 0.09-0.12 au, close to the dust sublimation radius (0.10-0.14 au for a sublimation temperature of about 1500 K). The Fe I emission is optically thick, whereas the optically thin Mg I lines imply 2.2 x 10^22 kg (3.6 x 10^-3 Earth masses) of magnesium gas in the ring. Conclusions: The dust and gas properties are consistent with a secondary origin involving collisions of rocky planetesimals. We propose that small collision-produced dust grains spiral inward and sublimate near the dust sublimation radius, accumulating atomic gas there. HD 152384 thus represents a young analogue of gas-bearing debris disks such as Beta Pictoris and gaseous debris disks around metal-polluted white dwarfs, offering a new window on the early violent processing of rocky planetesimals.

title: The physical and chemical structure of TMC-1. The spatial distribution and excitation conditions of carbon, oxygen, and sulfur bearing species: Depletion of CO and CS
summary: We present a detailed study of the physical and chemical structure of TMC-1 from the observed spatial distribution of HC3N, NNH+, CN, and their isotopologues, the O-bearing species C18O, C17O, CH3OH, CH3CHO, and H2CO, and the S-bearing species CS, HCS+, H2CS, and H2CCS. The well known filamentary structure of TMC-1 can be interpreted as a single cloud with a velocity gradient perpendicular to the filament, or less likely as due to the alignment of three independent clouds in the line sight with velocities of 5.3-5.7, 5.7-5.9, and 5.9-6.3 km/s. The main contribution to the emission of all studied C-bearing species is found at 5.83 kms/s. We conclude that the three velocity components are dynamically connected and that C-bearing molecules show a different behavior of their abundances compared to O-bearing species, which have emission peaks at 5.7 and 6.25 km/s, and appear at different spatial locations than cyanopolyynes and CnH and CnN radicals. The detection of 13C18O, with exactly the same line profile than that of C18O and C17O, excludes the possibility that the decrease of their emission at 5.83 km/s, could be due to self absorption or absorption by a foreground cloud component. Hence, as indicated by the spatial distribution of C18O and C17O, CO is significantly depleted at the velocities and positions where the emission of the carbon chains and radicals is found. This suggests that the emission of O-bearing species is coming from the external layers of the carbon-rich filaments. A comparison between S-bearing species and other molecules indicates that CS, CCS, HCS+, and H2CS are significantly depleted in the zone of CO depletion. A clear increase of the deuteration of several molecular species is found in the zones where CO and CS are depleted.

title: Starspots on weak-lined T Tauri stars in the sigma Orionis cluster
summary: The light curves and spectra of T Tauri stars indicate the presence of cool starspots covering large areas of their photospheres. Heavily spotted stars should have a larger mid-infrared flux than the equivalent single-temperature photospheres. To test this prediction we first fit single and two-temperature models to optical spectra of young stars in the 4 Myr-old sigma Orionis cluster and a control set of older field stars. The fits to the young stars favour two temperatures while the field stars show no preference. Independent tests of our models for nine probable single K-type weak-lined T Tauri stars using infrared photometry confirms the presence of large cool components. We consider and rule out as explanations of the two temperature photospheres: binary stars for all but one WTTS; accretion, as the observed H-alpha equivalent width is too small; gravity darkening as the predicted temperature differences are too small. This leaves cool areas akin to starspots covering 30-95 per cent of the surface as the plausible explanation. Our results show no significant difference in the cool temperature for surface fractions between 0.30-0.75, implying a common mechanism is responsible. These cool surface fractions would lead to significant overestimates in age and mass when fitting unspotted isochrones in colour-magnitude diagrams. The dispersion in cool surface fraction could also explain the dispersion in lithium equivalent width seen in the spectra of coeval zero-age main sequence stars.

title: Chandra-JWST Probing the Effects of Moderate X-Ray Superflares on Protoplanetary Disks
summary: Powerful X-ray flares from young stars may rapidly alter the physical and chemical conditions of their planet-forming disks, but direct observational tests remain scarce. We present a Chandra-JWST/NIRSpec study of infrared spectral variability associated with pre-main-sequence (PMS) X-ray flares in the Orion Nebula. Combining six Chandra/ACIS-I observations with three NIRSpec-MOS visits, we analyze two-epoch spectra of 10 X-ray Flare stars and 12 matched non-flaring Controls among 84 observed disk-bearing PMS stars. We investigate three diagnostics: narrow 2.8-4.3 micron features, HI Br-alpha, and the CO fundamental band. Flare stars show tentative evidence for relatively fewer variable narrow features at longer wavelengths than Controls, while feature incidence decreases strongly with projected distance from the dominant ionizing O star Theta1 Ori C. Most classifiable features appear in absorption. These properties suggest that at least some features may arise in externally irradiated disk atmospheres and/or associated photoevaporative flows, with their apparent epoch-to-epoch variability potentially reflecting spatial sampling of such locally structured material rather than intrinsic temporal changes. Br-alpha behaves differently: flare stars show systematically stronger variability and uniquely exhibit absorption-core profiles, suggesting control by magnetospheric accretion and stellar magnetic processes rather than disk irradiation. The CO fundamental band shows no significant flare-associated variability, consistent with thermochemical models predicting weak responses to moderate X-ray superflares. This pilot study demonstrates the potential of coordinated Chandra-JWST observations to probe how young stellar magnetic activity affects planet-forming environments, motivating future monitoring to build larger superflare samples and extend them into the rare X-ray mega-flare regime.

title: First L-type substellar object discovered in the vicinity of the embedded cluster NGC 2023
summary: We present the first substellar object in a star-forming region spectroscopically confirmed with Euclid, namely J054158.70-021031.4. This young and faint source is located close to the embedded open cluster NGC 2023. It has a spectral type of L3, a reddening of Av = 3 mag, proper motion consistent with the nearby cluster NGC 2024, and a magnitude of $\sim24.5$ in the Euclid optical band. At the distance of 403 pc, its inferred mass lies close to the planetary-mass boundary. We discovered the object by searching for ultracool dwarf candidates in the Euclid Early Release Observations. The search was based on photometric criteria, followed by the analysis of slitless 2D spectro-images in order to distinguish features that indicate the nature of these objects. This work demonstrates the potential of Euclid to unveil previously hidden populations of very low-mass objects, located in obscured regions where star formation is ongoing.

title: Probing Accretion and Outflow in V1180 Cas through High-Resolution Optical Spectroscopy
summary: We present an analysis of a high-resolution optical spectrum of V1180 Cas obtained with HIRES at the W. M. Keck Observatory during a bright photometric state of the source. The spectrum is dominated by strong emission lines, including H$α$, the Ca II infrared triplet, He I, and O I, along with numerous Fe I and Fe II transitions and several forbidden lines such as [O I] and [S II], indicating ongoing accretion and mass-loss activity. A weak Li I $λ$6708 absorption feature confirms the youth of the source. Using the Li I absorption and selected Fe I emission lines, we report for the first time a radial velocity of $-16 \pm 3$ km s$^{-1}$ for V1180 Cas. The H$α$ and H$β$ profiles exhibit asymmetric structures with blueshifted absorption components, suggesting outflowing material along the line of sight. The He I $λ$5876 line displays a narrow component likely associated with post-shock accretion regions and a broad, slightly blueshifted component probably arising from magnetospheric flows and/or inner disk winds. The [O I] $λ$6300 profile is decomposed into low- and high-velocity components, tracing a slow disk wind and a fast jet. Using the forbidden [O I] line, we estimate for the first time a disk inclination angle of $\approx50^\circ$. The derived mass accretion and jet mass-loss rates imply $\dot{M}_{jet}/\dot{M}_{acc} \sim 0.01$--$0.03$, at the lower end of, but consistent with, the range observed for Class II YSOs. Forbidden-line diagnostics indicate densities $\sim10^{3}$ and $10^{6}$ cm$^{-3}$ with temperatures of $\sim10^{4}$ K, supporting a multi-component outflow scenario. Overall, the results support a picture in which V1180 Cas is an actively accreting, moderately inclined system hosting a multi-component outflow.

title: Frontiers of chemical complexity in the interstellar medium: unveiling the cosmic origins of life
summary: The interstellar medium (ISM) contains a rich molecular inventory that provides a unique window into the chemistry operating during star and planet formation and its connection to prebiotic chemistry. More than 350 interstellar molecules are currently known, including increasingly complex organic molecules and species containing elements beyond the second row of the periodic table. Yet the limits that interstellar chemical complexity can reach, its evolution from molecular clouds to planetary systems, and its contribution to the molecular feedstock of life remain poorly constrained. Addressing these questions requires sensitive, broadband observations capable of detecting multiple weak rotational transitions of molecular species, such as amino acids, nucleobases, sugars and lipids, towards star- and planet-forming environments. Current facilities, including ALMA, are limited by instantaneous spectral coverage, sensitivity (especially on extended spatial scales), and the trade-off between total bandwidth and integration time. The proposed ALMA2040 facility would overcome these limitations through at least a tenfold improvement in spectral-line sensitivity, high-fidelity imaging from sub-arcsecond to tens-of-arcsecond scales, and ultra-broad instantaneous frequency coverage from 35 to 950 GHz at high spectral resolution. These capabilities would allow systematic detections of species with molecular abundances with respect to H$_2$ below 10$^{-11}$, facilitating the identification of new complex and heavy-element-bearing species through multiple transitions, and providing complete molecular inventories across evolutionary stages. ALMA2040 would thus make it possible to comprehensively investigate the emergence and evolution of chemical complexity, and to determine whether molecular precursors of prebiotic chemistry are widespread throughout the Galaxy.

title: Planetary system architectures in the final stages of planet formation
summary: The processes in the last stages of planet formation determine the final assembly and composition of planets. After the protoplanetary discs dissipate, a system of planets and planetesimals -- analogues of the Asteroid and Kuiper Belts -- remains. Ongoing collisions between these bodies produce second-generation dust and gas that form a debris disc. Resolved images of such belts allow us to trace the dynamical history of these systems, including giant impacts and planet-belt interactions, during the crucial era from 10 to a few 100 Myr of terrestrial planet formation. High-resolution mm and optical/near-IR imagers have revolutionised our view of the brightest planetesimal belts, providing first glimpses of diverse structures, many of which show plausible planet imprints, while ALMA has revealed gas in a growing number of systems. Yet these results are strongly biased toward the brightest, mostly young belts around early-type stars, and even for these, crucial details remain undetectable at the required resolution due to their typically low surface brightness. A future (sub-)mm facility with an order of magnitude leap in continuum sensitivity and 10x higher line sensitivity would transform our understanding of late-stage planet formation by enabling the first statistically meaningful surveys of faint outer planetesimal belts across all spectral types, imaging planetary collisions in the inner regions of planetary systems, and gas measurements that trace volatile delivery to terrestrial planets. For the first time, this would reach the faint majority of belts, rather than only the rare bright discs accessible today.

title: Planet formation on solar system scales
summary: Giant planets are often regarded as primordial protoplanetary "architects". Their formation and interactions with planetesimals and other planets during and after the protoplanetary disc phase are key to setting the blueprint of the planetary systems we observe today. Catching nascent gas giants is our best opportunity to uncover these crucial steps in the planet formation process and shed light on the origins of our own solar system. Over the last decade, ALMA has revolutionised our understanding of planet formation; still, detecting signatures of Jupiter-like planets has remained out of reach. We argue that ALMA2040, a next-generation sub(mm) interferometer with improved sensitivity ($\times25$ in the continuum and $\times10$ for line emission) and a $\times3$ higher angular resolution compared to ALMA, will be sensitive to (sub)mm emission around a forming Jupiter-like planet orbiting a Sun-like star within $150\,{\rm pc}$ and allow kinematically characterising interactions of Jovian and sub-Jovian planets with their natal disc. ALMA2040 will provide unique and unprecedented insights into how gas giants carve gaps, accrete material, form satellites, and affect the architectures of their co-evolving planetary systems.

title: The ALMA-QUARKS Survey. IV. Core Mass Function and Evolutionary Trends in Core Formation Efficiency and Chemistry
summary: The ALMA-QUARKS (Querying Underlying Mechanisms of Massive Star Formation with ALMA-Resolved Gas Kinematics and Structures) survey targets 139 massive protoclusters selected from the ATOMS survey. The targets were observed at 1.3~mm wavelength with an angular resolution of $\sim0.3^{\prime\prime}$, corresponding to $\sim10^3$~au at the sample's median distance of $\sim3.8$~kpc. Using \texttt{getsf}, we identify 3374 dense cores and classify them as starless, protostellar, hot core, or H{\sc ii} region candidates based on spectral-line diagnostics (e.g., H30$α$, CH$_3$CN, and CH$_3$OH) and CO outflow associations. The resulting catalog provides core physical properties and enables statistical investigations of dense core populations in massive protocluster environments. The derived global core mass function (CMF) after excluding H{\sc ii} region candidates, which is biased by distance effects, has a relatively flat power-law slope at the high-mass end ($\mathrm{d}N/\mathrm{d}\log M \propto M^{-γ}$, with $γ=0.98\pm0.03$). In contrast, the measured high-mass slopes in individual distance bins are approximately Salpeter-like, while their fitted lower mass limits increase with distance. We further examine the core formation efficiency (CFE) across the full sample and find that it positively correlates with the luminosity-to-mass ratio of the parental clumps, consistent with an evolutionary increase in the fraction of mass concentrated into dense cores. We also investigate the detection rates of different molecular tracers and find systematic chemical variations with evolutionary stage. Compared with the ASHES survey, we find that the detection rates of deuterated species vary significantly even for cores at the same evolutionary stages, suggesting an important environmental influence on the chemical evolution of cores.

title: Peering into the Midplane of the DM Tau Disk using N2H+ and DCO+
summary: Planets form in the midplanes of protoplanetary disks, thus investigating the properties of the midplane region can shed light on the physical and chemical processes governing the evolution of planetary systems. In this work, we study the conditions near the midplane of the disk around DM Tau using 0."3 (~43 au) ALMA observations of N2H+ (J = 3 - 2) and DCO+ (J = 4 - 3). The radial profiles reveal that DCO+ is centrally peaked, with a depression near 120 au, while N2H+ exhibits a central depression and a peak near 100 au. In addition, both molecules display extended emission out to 400 au. Using parametric models to interpret our observations, we note that a fiducial model based on CO-derived parameters captures the features within 200 au, but fails to reproduce the outer disk emission. We explore various mechanisms that could account for this extended emission and conclude that it is best reproduced by an increased external UV penetration and cosmic ray/X-ray ionization rate, possibly enhanced by radial drift. These processes affect the precursors of N2H+ and DCO+ : increased UV leads to the photodesorption of CO and N2, while ionization enhances H3+ abundance. Besides, the observed N2H+ and DCO+ features are broadly consistent with previous CO snowline constraints, but can also be shaped by processes such as ionization, CO depletion, and multiple chemical pathways. Thus, using these molecular ions as robust CO snowline tracers requires additional constraints from complementary molecular tracers and detailed chemical modeling.

title: The Milky Way's Early Disk Was Built in Bursts. I. Evidence from Low-angular-momentum, High-$α$ Stars Scattered Out of the Protodisk by Merger Events
summary: Stars born in the high-$α$ disk can later acquire low angular momentum through dynamical scattering during early merger events. Their age--metallicity distribution thus provides a fossil record of the history of both star formation and dynamical perturbations in the early Milky Way disk. Here we identify a sample of 2,078 such stars from more than two million Gaia DR3 subgiants with robust determinations of ages, kinematics, and abundances. From this sample we reconstruct their intrinsic age--metallicity distribution with a forward modeling approach. Our results confirm that these scattered stars are older and more metal-poor than the bulk of the high-$α$ disk on average. In particular, the joint age--metallicity distribution reveals a robust two-component feature: a broad, dominant component with a peak age of $\sim$11.5~Gyr and ${\rm [Fe/H]}\simeq-0.59$, and an older and more metal-poor component with a peak age of $\sim$12.5~Gyr and ${\rm [Fe/H]}\simeq-0.86$. The presence of this two-component structure suggests that the high-$α$ disk experienced episodic phases of star formation and chemical enrichment. The age distribution of the younger Splash component, compared with that of the high-$α$ disk, provides evidence for a substantial dynamical perturbation at a lookback time of 10.8--11.5~Gyr, possibly associated with an early passage of Gaia--Sausage--Enceladus (GSE). The older Splash component, with a peak age of $\sim$12.5~Gyr, may preserve signatures of an earlier interaction, possibly associated with the proposed Low-energy--Kraken--Heracles (LKH) event.

title: Resolving the thermal component of stellar feedback with the "anchor-and-refine" scheme in galactic simulations
summary: (abridged) Stellar feedback regulates galactic baryon cycles, but galaxy-scale simulations often cannot resolve supernova cooling radii. Momentum-based subgrid models can consequently underresolve the hot gas around young stars. We develop an "anchor-and-refine" feedback scheme that anchors a host cell near each star particle, preventing its displacement and preserving a thermal-feedback reservoir. When the cooling radius is resolved, all supernova energy is injected into the host cell as thermal energy; otherwise, the host cell is refined and terminal momentum is deposited into surrounding gas cells. Idealized tests agree with high-resolution simulations, yielding consistent superbubble properties and preserving hot interiors without artificial cooling. In an isolated Milky Way-mass galaxy, the scheme captures finer X-ray-emitting structures and a sharply defined, X-ray-bright central mid-plane. It also produces a smoother star formation history than pure hybrid feedback. Hot gas dominates outflow mass loading, with the mass-loading factor plateauing at approximately 0.2 at heights z>1 kpc. Phase decomposition indicates that hot gas sustains a steady, energy-driven wind, whereas cooler outflows decline with height because of radiative cooling and gravitational fallback. These results highlight the role of thermal feedback in driving galactic winds. By preserving hot superbubble interiors and the partition of thermal and kinetic energy, anchor-and-refine improves the treatment of hot gas, star formation, and feedback at limited resolution, supporting future applications to galaxy-scale and cosmological zoom-in simulations.

title: Testing Pre-main-sequence Evolutionary Models with Gaia and SPHEREx Observations of Canis Major North
summary: Pre-main-sequence (PMS) evolutionary models can assign different ages across stellar mass within the same population. We use joint Gaia and SPHEREx spectral energy distributions to infer effective temperatures, radii, and luminosities for members of Canis Major North (CMaN), a nearby association with independent lithium and kinematic age constraints near 23 Myr. The SPHEREx fluxes agree with 2MASS and WISE photometry to 3--6\%, and we anchor the absolute flux scale to Gaia, 2MASS, and WISE. Using the revised temperatures, we obtain a lithium age of $22.4^{+2.8}_{-1.5}$ Myr. For a 29-star PMS sample, population-wide HR-diagram fits yield $20.5^{+1.5}_{-1.4}$ Myr for unspotted SPOTS models, consistent with the external constraints, $18.4^{+1.4}_{-1.3}$ and $18.7^{+1.3}_{-1.2}$ Myr for the Feiden nonmagnetic and BHAC15 models, and substantially older ages of $32.2^{+2.3}_{-2.1}$ and $55^{+5}_{-5}$ Myr for the Feiden magnetic and PARSEC models. No grid returns a temperature-independent age. The Feiden, SPOTS, and BHAC15 models assign older ages to stars above $4000$ K, whereas PARSEC assigns increasingly older ages toward lower temperatures. The intrinsic luminosity dispersion is also mass dependent, approximately $0.14$ dex below $3450$ K but $0.05$ dex at intermediate temperatures. At a fixed age of 23.0 Myr, a single SPOTS filling factor cannot reproduce the width of the low-temperature sequence, whereas the empirical filling-factor distribution of young stars overpredicts it. Spotted isochrones can enclose every cool member only at ages of 37--50 Myr, inconsistent with the lithium and kinematic ages.

title: Stellar Kinematics and Molecular Gas toward NGC 6357: An Overlooked Earlier Stellar Generation
summary: We investigate past star formation in NGC 6357 using Gaia DR3 astrometry and Three-mm Ultimate Mopra Milky Way Survey (ThrUMMS) $^{12}$CO($J=1$--0) data. A Hierarchical Density-Based Spatial Clustering of Applications with Noise (HDBSCAN) search independently recovers the previously cataloged cluster G352.8+0.6 in addition to Pismis 24, G353.1+0.6, and G353.2+0.6. Isochrone fitting yields an age of $7.9^{+1.5}_{-1.4}$ Myr for G352.8+0.6, compared with approximately 1--3 Myr for the three young clusters. Assuming constant relative plane-of-sky motion, a linear traceback places G352.8+0.6 closest to their reference center approximately 1.8 Myr ago, comparable to their inferred ages. The $+2$ km s$^{-1}$ CO component overlaps G352.8+0.6 in projection and shows localized depressions in integrated intensity around three spectroscopically identified massive stars belonging to G352.8+0.6. The $-4$ and $+2$ km s$^{-1}$ components show complementary projected distributions and intermediate-velocity CO emission in position--velocity space. Assuming that the $+2$ km s$^{-1}$ component was physically associated with G352.8+0.6 and shared its transverse motion, our principal interpretation is that the two molecular structures interacted around the epoch indicated by the stellar traceback, approximately 1.8 Myr ago. The resulting gas compression may have contributed to the recent episode of clustered and high-mass star formation in NGC 6357 and to the formation of Shell A, which subsequent stellar feedback may have reshaped.

title: Unveiling the Shock-Excited Molecular Environment in the Orion Protostar HOPS 370
summary: We present near-infrared K-band ($1.94$--$2.52~μ$m) spectroscopy of the deeply embedded protostellar source HOPS\,370, obtained with the TIFR--ARIES Near Infrared Spectrometer (TANSPEC) on the 3.6-m Devasthal Optical Telescope (DOT). The spectrum is dominated by prominent molecular hydrogen ($\rm H_2$) ro-vibrational emission, with multiple transitions detected from the $1$--$0$ S, $2$--$1$ S, and $1$--$0$ Q branches. Using the intrinsically linked $\rm H_2$ $1$--$0$ Q(3) and $1$--$0$ S(1) transitions, which arise from the same upper energy level, we derive a visual extinction of $A_V = 23.24 \pm 1.25$ mag, corresponding to $A_K = 2.50 \pm 0.13$ mag, consistent with the embedded Class~0/I nature of the source. The diagnostic line ratio $F(2$--$1~{\rm S}(1))/F(1$--$0~{\rm S}(1)) = 0.12 \pm 0.01$ is consistent with thermal excitation and disfavors ultraviolet fluorescence as the dominant excitation mechanism. Assuming optically thin emission and local thermodynamic equilibrium, we derive an $\rm H_2$ excitation diagram that yields an excitation temperature of $2078 \pm 215$ K and a molecular hydrogen column density of $(1.93 \pm 0.93)\times10^{20}$ cm$^{-2}$. We further derive an ortho-to-para ratio of $2.45 \pm 0.21$, indicating substantial shock-driven thermal processing while remaining below the high-temperature equilibrium value of 3. Taken together, these diagnostics indicate that the molecular hydrogen emission in HOPS\,370 originates predominantly in warm, shock-heated gas most likely associated with its protostellar outflow. Our results demonstrate the diagnostic power of combined S- and Q-branch $\rm H_2$ spectroscopy for constraining the physical conditions and excitation history of deeply embedded protostellar systems.

title: Tentative Detection of FeS toward Orion SrcI
summary: Iron sulfide (FeS) is a key refractory compound in astrophysical environments. It is commonly found in meteorites and evidence of FeS has only been reported in solid form in a protoplanetary environment. Furthermore, FeS is of astrobiological interest since it acts as a precursor to the formation of pyrite (FeS$_2$), which plays a key role in anaerobic metabolism. We present millimeter-wave spectroscopic calculations for gaseous FeS and report its tentative detection toward the massive disk Orion SrcI. If confirmed, this would constitute the first ever detection of gaseous FeS in the interstellar medium. Our data are consistent with a FeS column density of $\sim1.7 \times 10^{15}$ cm$^{-2}$. Comparing to other sulfur reservoirs, the amount of sulfur locked in FeS is more than three orders of magnitude lower than that contained in SO$_2$ and SiS. However, FeS emission may arise from a different region as it is the case for the metallic salt NaCl. Our results support the presence of FeS in interstellar grains and are consistent with grain destruction playing an important role in the origin of the FeS emission. The observations, however, are still insufficient to discern whether FeS is a main sulfur reservoir in molecular clouds or a primary carrier of refractory iron-bearing material.

title: Water Abundance and Ortho-Para Ratio in the S140 Photon Dominated Region
summary: We analyzed archival far-infrared to submillimeter Herschel PACS, SPIRE, and HIFI spectroscopic observations of the S140 photon dominated region (PDR) to constrain the water vapor abundance and ortho-para ratio in this region. Toward the high-mass protostar IRS1, 52 spectral lines, including 15 water lines, are detected with the PACS and SPIRE instruments. PDR modeling suggests a UV radiation field G0 ~ 1 x 10^3 Habing units, and a thermal gas pressure of 5 x 10^8 K cm^-3 in this region. The models strongly underestimate intensities of high-J CO lines, which may indicate the presence of hot shocked gas associated with outflows along the line of sight, in addition to the UV irradiated gas. The spectral resolution of the PACS and SPIRE spectrometers is insufficient to separate the PDR and shock contributions. The PDR models further suggest that optically thick ground-state water lines trace primarily surface layers of the PDR. The gas temperature in this region is predicted to be ~ 800 K and the water abundance with respect to hydrogen nuclei reaches ~ 10^-5. However, the bulk of gas-phase water is located in a more shielded region, deeper inside the PDR, with a gas temperature ~ 24 K, and a gas-phase H_2O abundance of ~ 10^-7. A comparison of the observed water line fluxes toward IRS1 with PDR model predictions shows no evidence for departures from the LTE ortho-para ratio at the local gas temperature, which is assumed in the models. The sensitivity of the Herschel instruments was insufficient to measure the water ortho-para ratio toward the externally illuminated edge-on PDR at the surface of the S140 molecular cloud. Such observations will be possible with the next generation far-infrared spectroscopic space missions currently in development.

title: Chemical complexity in feedback from supernova remnants: first detection of PO+ in IC443 and W44
summary: Supernova remnant (SNR) may shape the physical and chemical properties of star formation. By releasing refractory elements into the gas phase, they inject material of pre-biotic relevance into molecular clouds. Such elements may be inherited by planetary systems and become relevant for the emergence of life. We investigate the presence of P-bearing species in molecular clouds impacted by SNR-shocks. P is a crucial biological element, but its presence and reservoir in molecular clouds remain elusive. We present high-sensitivity 3 mm observations obtained with the IRAM 30m, toward the interaction sites between the SNRs W44 and IC443 and their associated molecular clouds. Focusing on PO+(2-1) and PN(2-1), we derive molecular column densities and abundances in local thermodynamic equilibrium. We investigate the correlation between P-bearing species and the shock tracer Silicon Monoxide (SiO). We detect, for the first time, PO+ toward SNRs, with abundances X(PO+)~8e-12-5e-11, but no significant PN emission. PO+ toward both SNRs is associated with strong SiO emission, showing similar linewidths but velocity offsets, suggesting that PO+ preferentially traces the most compressed and more strongly ionised layers of the shock. By comparing the derived abundances with those reported in literature, we suggest that the PO+ abundance mainly depends on a combination of shock strength and shocked medium density. Our results indicate that P-chemistry in SNR shocks is shifted toward an ion-dominated regime, likely driven by enhanced cosmic-ray ionisation rates. In this scenario, neutral species such as PN are efficiently destroyed, while ion-molecule reactions favour the production of PO+. This suggests that SNR shocks may play a role in processing P-bearing material and shaping gas-phase P chemistry in molecular clouds, with potential implications for the chemical inventory of star-forming environments.

title: Complex Organic Molecules in Protostars with ALMA Spectral Surveys (COMPASS) VII. First interstellar detection of fully deuterated methanol
summary: There have been no robust identifications of fully deuterated methanol, CD3OD, in the interstellar medium (ISM) to date. Our goal is continue the search for CD3OD in star-forming regions to determine the deuteration pattern of methanol and set constraints on the deuteration process. We used a sensitive imaging spectral survey of the protostellar system IRAS4A in the NGC1333 molecular cloud performed as part of the large program carried out with the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) called Complex Organic Molecules in Protostars with ALMA Spectral Surveys (COMPASS). The column densities of methanol and several of its less abundant isotopologs, including deuterated ones, were derived under the assumption of local thermodynamic equilibrium (LTE). Along with the detection of several methanol isotopologs toward the binary component IRAS4A2, we report the first interstellar detection of CD3OD. The deuteration pattern of methanol in IRAS4A2 is similar to the pattern measured in other low-mass protostars, with an increase in the apparent D/H ratio from the singly to multiply deuterated isotopologs. Chemical models of prestellar and protostellar cores focused on deuteration do not reproduce this pattern quantitatively. This discrepancy is even more exacerbated by the detection of CD3OD. Our LTE modeling of the spectra yields low column density ratios of methanol to its 13C and 18O isotopologs while the 13C to 18O and 18O to 17O ratios are consistent with the isotopic ratios expected in the local ISM. We suspect that the column density of methanol is underestimated. One possible explanation is that the emission is clumpy rather than monolithic. The first detection of a fully deuterated COM highlights the power of deuterium fractionation as a diagnostic tool for investigating the formation and inheritance of organic molecules during the process of star formation.

title: A comparison between particle and fluid approaches for streaming instability in global patch simulations
summary: Identifying the process relevant to planet formation is still a major task. Mechanisms have been identified that can trap dust, preventing it from migrating inwards. A particular hydrodynamic instability, known as the streaming instability, is of high interest because it may be responsible for the formation of dust clumps from which the first planetesimals form. We aim to compare the outcome of non-linear streaming instability simulations using both fundamental approaches in a more realistic global disk model. The results will not be used to identify or disentangle the effect of, e.g., numerical diffusion in fluid simulations or the possibility of having crossing particle streams. Instead, they will enable us to determine whether the Lagrangian particle approach is the most suitable for numerical studies of the streaming instability. Methods: We perform 2D, axisymmetric, global, and isothermal hydrodynamic simulations using the two codes FARGO3D (dust fluid) and PLUTO (fluid, particles) to investigate the temporal evolution of dust scale height, midplane dust-to-gas ratio, and maximum dust density as well as to study velocity distributions and vorticities. For PLUTO particle simulations, we also investigate the influence of the gas Riemann solver and spatial reconstruction orders. Our results from a resolution study up to 5120 cells per gas scale height indicate convergence between PLUTO fluid and FARGO3D. Both yield a Gaussian profile dominated by small-scale, dust-depleted voids. Particle simulations with PLUTO have not yet converged, as a transient midplane dust component persists, indicating the need for even higher resolution or more particles. Using a more accurate Riemann solver or a higher-order spatial reconstruction scheme helps to bring the dust density profile closer to the converged structure.

title: Ultraviolet accretion continua reveal a transition in T Tauri magnetic topology
summary:
Magnetic fields regulate accretion in T Tauri stars (TTSs) and evolve as radiative cores emerge during pre-main-sequence contraction. Stars above ~0.35-0.5 Msun transition from fully convective to partially convective interiors, a change associated with increasingly complex magnetic topologies and evolving dynamo behaviour. Because accretion flows are magnetically channelled, this evolution is expected to modify ultraviolet (UV) accretion diagnostics, although observational evidence has remained limited.
  We identify a transition in the UV continuum properties of TTSs using archival International Ultraviolet Explorer observations, complemented by recent spectra from the Hubble Space Telescope ULLYSES survey. An empirical UV photospheric sequence constructed from G-M main-sequence stars shows that late K-M TTSs broadly follow standard photosphere-plus-shock model predictions, whereas G-K5 stars display systematically lower F270/F303 continuum flux ratios (flux at 270 nm relative to 303 nm).
  Statistical analysis shows that transition models describe the observations significantly better than a single continuous trend, locating the transition near spectral type K5-K6, with its precise location limited by spectral-classification uncertainties, and consistent with the fully convective boundary. Comparison with photosphere-plus-shock models further shows that, while the late-type population is broadly encompassed by the parameter space sampled by the adopted models, the warmer stars extend systematically beyond it in this UV diagnostic.
  We interpret this transition as evidence for a change in magnetospheric accretion associated with the evolution of magnetic topology across the radiative-core boundary, resulting in a corresponding change in the emergent UV continuum.

title: Star spots mimic the proposed abundance signatures of planet formation
summary: Trends with stellar elemental abundances and condensation temperature have been proposed as a possible tracer of rocky planet formation. Here we present an alternative explanation, where we show that stellar activity (star spots) can also cause apparent abundance changes in refractory elements preferentially over volatile elements. This effect arises naturally from atomic physics: refractory (rocky; high-$T_c$) elements preferentially have low first-ionization potentials, with strong transitions that are most sensitive to the cooler, magnetically-perturbed spot conditions, making any spot-induced change in line strength correlated with $T_c$. We re-examine literature on Sun-like stars in the Solar neighborhood and find that the $\log{R'_{HK}}$ stellar activity indicator is correlated with the so-called $T_c$ slope: the gradient of chemical abundances with respect to condensation temperature. Using 1D LTE Korg.jl simulations of the Sun with spots of varying size and contrast, we show that a wide range of spot configurations can manifest as abundance patterns that mimic a signal of abundance trends with condensation temperature. Finally, we conduct a line-by-line differential analysis of an ambient Solar spectrum relative to a Solar sunspot umbra to represent an extreme case, where we find that elements with high condensation temperature can show a factor of three (0.5 dex) increase. We discuss implications that stellar activity poses for precision spectroscopy, and provide some direction on how this effect might be mitigated.

title: B-fields In STar-forming Region Observations (BISTRO): Dual-Wavelength Constraints on Size-Dependent Grain Alignment in Star-Forming Regions
summary: We compared 450 and 850 $μ$m POL-2 observations from the James Clerk Maxwell Telescope at $12.6''$ resolution. The median absolute difference in polarization angle between bands is $6.7^\circ$ across 21 regions. For total intensity $I\proptoν^α$ and polarized intensity $PI\proptoν^γ$, 24-27 of 35 regions have $γ<α$, allowing for $3σ$ limits on weak polarized intensities. The median $γ-α$ is $-0.51$, ranging from $-0.57$ to $-0.45$ under these limits. The ratio of polarization fractions is $P_{450}/P_{850}=0.69\pm0.02_{\rm sys}\pm0.03_{\rm stat}$, with no detected dependence on the angle difference. We suggest that the dependence of alignment on grain size offers the simplest explanation of these findings. For optically thin components sharing a polarization angle and opacity law, temperature mixing reproduces the median $-0.51$ only if the warm dust is polarized less efficiently than the cold dust. If the cold dust is at 10 K or warmer and the warm dust at 40 K or cooler, the median requires a ratio of warm to cold effective polarization efficiencies $r\lesssim0.18$. We tested mixtures with opacity index $β=2$ in four fields against Herschel dust temperatures and Green Bank Ammonia Survey kinetic temperatures. We assumed equal gas and dust temperatures, ammonia tracing cold gas, and model ranges of 3-20 K for cold dust and 25-40 K for warm dust carrying at most half the mass. Mixtures matching both temperatures cannot reproduce $γ-α$ within $1σ$ in three fields, including OMC 2 tentatively, even for $r=0$. Allowing warm dust at 10-100 K and up to 95% of the mass permits solutions only for $r\leq0.041$. To explain these three fields by temperature mixing, we need wider model ranges and a very strong contrast in polarization efficiency. The origin of this contrast remains undetermined.

title: Rotation in the Lagoon Nebula with K2
summary: A low-mass star's rotation rate drives its magnetic field, and in the case of young stars, also affects accretion and planetary formation. Observations of the rotation rates of young stars help constrain models of star and planet formation. We present rotation rates from K2 observations of stars in the ~1-2 Myr Lagoon Nebula, one of the youngest clusters with space-based rotation rates available. From 414 light curves we obtain reliable rotation periods for 325 stars; 124 of them are disk-bearing and 201 are disk-free. This constitutes a significant increase in the collection of K2 rotation rates available for ~1-5 Myr stars. The overall distribution is broadly consistent with expectations, in that the slowest rotators are mid-K and both lower and higher masses are on average faster rotating. There is weak evidence that disked stars rotate more slowly. There are a few complex periodic variables, but they appear to be surprisingly high mass compared to prior known examples of this kind of object.

title: Optical-Infrared Extinction Variation in Nearby Molecular Clouds
summary: The dust extinction curve is an important probe of the properties of dust grains, particularly their size distribution. The properties of dust grains are expected to change significantly in dense molecular clouds due to shielding from interstellar radiation and increased frequency of grain-grain and grain-gas collisions. We measure the dust extinction curve shape parameter R(V) in 9 nearby, dense molecular clouds using data from the APOGEE spectroscopic survey, in combination with ten-band photometry from PS1, 2MASS, and WISE. We analyze the results to determine how the extinction curve varies in nearby molecular clouds. We find that most molecular clouds show a positive correlation between R(V) and E(B-V), but the strength of the correlation varies significantly between clouds. In addition, we find that the clouds with the strongest correlation tend to have very high dispersion in R(V) at fixed E(B-V), which tightens dramatically when clouds are subdivided into separate regions. This suggests that local environmental conditions beyond density shape the R(V)-E(B-V) relation.

title: The 200-300 GHz Survey for 18 Class II Disks in the Ophiuchus Star-Forming Complex
summary: We measured the 198-310 GHz flux densities of 18 Class II protoplanetary disks in the Ophiuchus star-forming complex using the Submillimeter Array (SMA). The $\sim$200-300 GHz spectral indices ($α_{200-300}$) of these disks are $2.3^{+0.2}_{-0.5}$. In this observed frequency range, emission properties of the Ophiuchus disks are very similar to the 48 spatially compact Class II disks in the Taurus-Auriga region observed in a previous SMA survey. Combining the Ophiuchus and Taurus-Auriga samples, the Pearson correlation coefficient between $α_{200-300}$ and the flux density at 250 GHz ($F_{250\,\mathrm{GHz}}$) is 0.27 ($p=0.02$). We do not find a convincing correlation between $α_{200-300}$ and the $R_{95\%}$ radius of the disks. Our interpretation for the $α_{200-300}$ values being close to 2 in the spatially compact disks is that at $\gtrsim 200$ GHz frequencies, the continuum emission in these disks is dominated by optically thick dust thermal emission, independent of $F_{250\,\mathrm{GHz}}$ and $R_{95\%}$. As a result, the (sub)millimeter luminosity and the apparent disk size are positively correlated, which has been found in numerous resolved emission surveys of Class II disks. In young clusters with ages of $\sim$1-2 Myr, Class II disks with smaller radii or lower (sub)millimeter luminosities are not necessarily those in which the dust mass budget has been consumed or dispersed.

title: Spatial distribution of water ice in the protoplanetary silhouette disk d216-0939
summary: The composition of rocky planets depends on the dust in their natal protoplanetary disk (PPD), potentially containing water ice. Crystalline water ice was detected in the PPD d216-0939 in the Orion Nebular Cluster (ONC). We aim at constraining the spatial distribution and crystallization state of water ice in the d216-0939 disk using recent observations of the water ice absorption feature at a wavelength of $\sim 3\mathrm{μm}$ collected with JWST. We perform 3D Monte Carlo radiative transfer (MCRT) simulations to constrain the free parameters of an accretion disk model by fitting the calculated spectrum in the wavelength range from $1.6 \text{ to } 24\mathrm{μm}$ to the spectral energy distribution (SED) observed with the JWST instruments NIRSpec and MIRI. Additionally, archival, spatially resolved HST observations were used to constrain the global spatial structure of the disk, as the parameter space is degenerate with respect to the fit to the SED. Successively, we fit the water ice absorption feature using polychromatic MCRT simulations with spectral importance sampling to produce synthetic observations at high spectral resolutions. By probing the upper and outer disk layers, we found that a PPD model with dust containing 5.4% crystallized water ice beyond the snowline fits the observations well, necessitating outward transport of material, since crystalline ice is unlikely to form in situ in the probed disk layers. In the spectral region of the water ice absorption feature, scattering and thermal dust emission both contribute significantly to the total flux.

title: A breath of fresh air: Oxygen enhancement from silicate sublimation during early protostellar evolution
summary: Recently, an analog to the t = 0 moment of our Solar System's meteoritic record was identified for the first time around the Class I protostar HOPS-315. Crystalline silicates were found to recondense from SiO gas that cools as it advects upward from a hot thermostat region in the inner midplane. This t=0 moment may be associated with the formation of the first planetesimals in this disk. We explore whether HOPS-68, a Class I protostar with similar properties and system geometries, is engaged in such refractory recondensation as well. A detection of cooler gas-phase SiO in absorption above a hot disk midplane would allow us to achieve this goal, thanks to a previous detection of crystalline silicates. HOPS-68 was observed with the JWST MIRI and NIRSpec, showing multiple bands of molecular absorption. We use local thermal equilibrium slab models to measure the temperature, column density, velocity, and radial location of these bands. The molecular absorption bands of gaseous SiO, H2O, CO2, and 13CO trace a warm molecular inversion layer (300-500 K) at mid-altitudes above the hot disk midplane from 0.3-16 AU, which is consistently blue-shifted with respect to the system velocity by 33-53 km/s. Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) observations of HOPS-68 kinematically resolve an SiO-rich jet and wind. We confirm that HOPS-68, like HOPS-315, is undergoing an epoch analogous to the t=0 moment in the Solar System's planet formation timeline. The detected warm molecular layer traces the base of a disk wind, which carries sublimated material from the thermostat region near 2 AU up into the outer disk. As for HOPS-315, the molecular layer in the inner few AU of HOPS-68 is enhanced in bulk oxygen as a result of this sublimation. Since HOPS-68 is less evolved than HOPS-315, this may indicate a prolonged epoch in protostellar evolution in which such oxygen enhancement occurs.

title: Complex Organic Molecules in Protostars with ALMA Spectral Surveys (COMPASS) -- IV. Methyl cyanide isotopologues toward BHR71-IRS1
summary: Methyl cyanide is one of the most abundant nitrogen-bearing complex organic molecules observed in the gas phase around low- and high-mass protostars. However, very few observations exist with a broad enough frequency coverage and sufficiently high sensitivity to systematically characterize its minor isotopologues toward such regions. We add to this number by analyzing data toward BHR71-IRS1 taken as part of the Complex Organic Molecules in Protostars with ALMA Spectral Surveys (COMPASS) Large Program over a ~33 GHz frequency range. We studied as many isotopologues of methyl cyanide as possible toward BHR71-IRS1. We found the column densities and excitation temperatures via spectral fitting and assuming local thermodynamic equilibrium. We then compared the derived column density ratios with those toward IRAS 16293-2422 A and B, V883 Ori, G31.41+0.31, and Sgr B2(N2b). We detect CH3CN, CH3CN $v_8$=1, 13-CH3CN, CH3-13-CN, CH3C-15-N, CH2DCN, and CHD2CN. The column density ratio of 13-CH3CN/CH3-13-CN is around unity, in agreement with previous observations. The CH2DCN/CH3CN ratios are similar for all the low-mass objects but are ~1 order of magnitude higher than those toward Sgr B2(N2b). This could be due to a warmer pre-stellar phase or a different formation timescale of Sgr B2(N2b). The D/H ratios found from methyl cyanide isotopologues agree well with those of methanol toward BHR71-IRS1, likely pointing to the formation and deuteration of methyl cyanide in a similar star-formation phase as methanol (i.e., the pre-stellar phase). We find an increase in the methyl cyanide D/H ratios with the number of deuterium atoms, which suggests that the deuterated isotopologues may form later in the pre-stellar phase. Future COMPASS studies will increase the sample size of low-mass systems with methyl cyanide analysis and potentially examine some of the trends observed here statistically.

title: JWST Imaging of Edge-on Protoplanetary Disks. V. Flux Ratio Reversal and Disk-edge Structure in the Flying Saucer
summary: We present near- and mid-infrared broadband imaging observations of the edge-on protoplanetary disk 2MASS J16281370-2431391, a.k.a. the 'Flying Saucer', obtained with NIRCam and MIRI on board JWST. These data are combined with archival optical and near-IR broadband imaging from HST, millimeter dust continuum emission from ALMA, and optical lightcurves from the K2 and TESS for a comprehensive multi-wavelength study. The JWST observations reveal a reversal of the flux ratio between the two reflection nebulae at near-infrared wavelengths (2-3 $μm$), which can be explained by a misaligned inner disk. For the first time, JWST reveals the bright lining along the disk edge at 2 and 3 $μm$, arising from forward scattering of background photons by dust grains near the $τ\approx 1$ layer. By combining the dust lane thickness measured with HST and JWST, we find the dust grains up to at least $\sim$3$μ$m are vertically mixed throughout the disk and have undergone significant growth. In addition, comparison of earlier HST/NICMOS J and K band images with those from JWST/NIRCam reveals variability in the scattered-light morphology, as well as measurable proper motion of the system with respect to the background stars, confirming that the Flying Saucer is co-moving with the young star population of $ρ$ Ophiuchi.

title: A Search for Dust in the Outflow of the HH212 Class 0 Protostellar System
summary: Perhaps the most visually striking phenomenon during star formation is the ejection of material along the direction of the protostar's rotational axis. Observed in the form of molecular outflows and/or atomic jets, these features carry away mass, energy and angular momentum from the system. Given the known dust content of protoplanetary disks, and the energetics of outflows, it has been suggested that it should be possible to lift dust from disks via winds, yet limited observational evidence has been presented in the literature. Any detection of dust within protostellar outflows not only puts constraints on the dust content in outflows, but if a sufficient amount of dust can be removed from the system, the mass budget for planet formation could also be affected. We present re-imaging of archival, multi-frequency dust continuum observations taken with the Atacama Large Millimeter/sub-millimeter Array (ALMA) towards the HH212 protostellar system. We detect an extension in the dust emission, and using multi-frequency data in Bands 7 and 9, we estimate the spectral index of the emitting dust and the dust mass in the wind launching region. We find a small but still significant amount of dust mass coincident with the molecular outflow cavity. This finding is assessed in relation to the hypothesis that the outflow could be capable of transporting dust away from the HH212 protoplanetary disk.

title: Unveiling star formation at sub-solar metallicity with ALMA2040
summary: A fundamental question in astrophysics is whether the processes governing star formation are universal or depend on the physical conditions of their local galactic environment. The Milky Way and the Magellanic clouds offer ideal laboratories to explore this question, as the gas conditions in them span up to orders of magnitude in metallicity, gas surface density, ambient pressure, dust abundance, radiation field, and cosmic-ray flux. In particular, both the outer Milky Way and the Magellanic clouds provide the closest low-metallicity environments with conditions similar to those of metal-poor galaxies, while remaining sufficiently close to soon allow spatial resolution of individual star-forming cores and disks. Recent observations with ALMA and other facilities have begun to unveil the physical and chemical properties of star-forming regions in low-metallicity environments. Yet, their distances from the Sun still require transformational gains in current ALMA capabilities to address fundamental open questions: (1) Are the properties of prestellar cores universal? (2) Does cloud fragmentation, and the resulting stellar IMF, depend critically on metallicity? (3) How does dust evolution depend on metallicity, and what is the impact in the survival of protoplanetary disks? (4) Is the reduced amount of metals and dust shielding at low metallicity critical for the formation and survival of molecules? ALMA2040 will identify similarities and differences between solar- and sub-solar-metallicity star-forming regions, and answer the question: how do different environmental conditions influence the physical and chemical pathways leading to star formation?

title: Thermodynamics of Viscously Heated Circumplanetary Disks
summary: Circumplanetary disks (CPDs) play an important role in the formation of gas giants and their satellites, yet remain poorly understood owing to the lack of observables and comprehensive theoretical models. Incorporating $α$-viscosity, a free-fall prescription of mass infall and boundary layer accretion, we develop an axisymmetric viscous radiation hydrodynamic (RHD) model. We evolve this model for different physical parameters using the RHD code {\tt Guangqi}, which solves RHD equations under the flux-limited diffusion approximation. In eight out of nine simulations, we obtain quasi-steady-state solutions and verify self-consistent energy conversion and transport. Overall, disk thickness increases with accretion rate and decreases with planet mass, consistent with the expected trend in conventional $α$-disk models. On the other hand, we highlight that the boundary layer plays a significant role in setting angular momentum transport and thermodynamics of the inner CPD, yielding ``hot'' ($s_{\rm real}>11\,k_{\rm{B}}\,m_{\rm{H}}^{-1}$) accreted gas, and potentially leading to dust sublimation. We identify a supersonic accretion flow, amounting to $2\%$--$5\%$ of the total accretion rate, located at high elevations above the CPDs with low angular momentum in our simulations. If the planet is massive ($\gtrsim3\,M_{\rm J}$), this low angular momentum flow impacting the planetary surface could generate observable H$α$ emission when the shock accretion rate is $\gtrsim5.5\times10^{-8}\, M_{\rm J}\,\rm{yr}^{-1}$.

title: The Birth and Early Feedback of Massive Star Clusters Across the Local Universe
summary: Young massive star clusters (YMCs; ${\gtrsim}10^4\rm\,M_\odot$) represent a distinct, extreme mode of star formation and the closest present-day analogues of the environments in which globular clusters and Cosmic Noon stellar populations assembled. Given the extreme dust extinction in the earliest phase of YMC formation, (sub-)millimeter observations are the only means of probing their assembly and early feedback.
